opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that formalization is a translation problem, and translation is never neutral. When a mathematician writes a theorem on paper, there's an enormous amount of shared context doing silent work: conventions about what "natural number" means, whether zero is included, what's implicitly assumed to be finite, what "generic" means in a given subfield. Lean doesn't have any of that. Every assumption has to be stated, and the moment you state it, you've made a choice that may or may not match what the author meant.

So the first problem is fidelity. It's surprisingly easy to write a Lean statement that type-checks, looks plausible, and is actually a different theorem. Sometimes it's subtly weaker, sometimes it's vacuous. A classic failure mode is a hypothesis that can never be satisfied, so the "theorem" is trivially true. Or division by zero being defined as zero in Lean, which can quietly change the meaning of a statement. A proof checker will happily verify a proof of the wrong thing. Lean guarantees the proof is correct relative to the statement; it can't guarantee the statement is what you wanted. That gap is where most of the human judgment lives.

The second problem is the library. Mathlib is extraordinary, but it reflects particular design decisions about how objects are represented: typeclasses, coercions, the choice between bundled and unbundled structures. If your problem lives in an area Mathlib covers well, specifying it can be smooth. If it touches something that isn't there yet, or is there in an awkward form, you end up building scaffolding before you can even state the problem. And the "natural" way a mathematician phrases something often isn't the way that plays nicely with the library, so there's a tension between faithfulness to the informal statement and usability for proving.

Third, there's the issue of what counts as an answer. For competition-style problems, a lot of questions are "find all x such that..." or "determine the maximum value." Specifying that formally is genuinely tricky, because you have to encode the answer into the statement, and then you have to decide what form of the answer is acceptable. Is a closed form required? Is an equivalent but unsimplified expression fine? If you're not careful, you can make the problem trivial by letting the answer be "the set of all x satisfying the condition."

And finally, it's a scarce skill. The people who are both strong research mathematicians and fluent Lean formalizers are a small community. Checking that a formal statement matches an informal one still largely requires that rare combination of expertise. That's part of why I think autoformalization, getting AI to do this translation reliably and to flag its own uncertainty, is one of the most important problems in the space. If we want verified mathematics to scale, specification can't remain the bottleneck. The proving side gets a lot of attention, but in some ways the statement side is the harder and more foundational problem.

r001.rationale: The response says Lean requires every assumption to be stated and discusses choosing definitions and conventions such as what counts as a natural number or finite, identifying this specification work as a difficulty before proof.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the hard part is that Lean forces you to say exactly what you mean, and most mathematics as it's actually written doesn't do that. When a mathematician states a problem, there's a huge amount of shared context sitting underneath it. What "a function" means, which domain you're on, whether zero counts as a natural number, what "the solutions" refers to. Humans fill that in automatically. Lean doesn't fill anything in. Every object has to be constructed from a specific type, and every assumption has to be stated explicitly, or the theorem you've written is not the theorem you meant.

So the first difficulty is just translation. You take something like "find all integers n such that..." and you realize that in Lean you can't say "find." You have to turn it into a statement: the set of such n equals exactly this set. And that already changes the problem, because now the answer is baked into the specification. If you get the answer slightly wrong, or you mischaracterize the set, you've written a false theorem, and no amount of proving will save you.

The second difficulty is what I'd call silent mis-formalization. The scary cases aren't the ones where Lean complains. Those are easy, you fix the type error. The scary cases are the ones where Lean accepts your statement, it looks right, you prove it, and it's actually vacuous. You divided by something that could be zero and Lean's division returns zero there, so the statement became trivial. Or you quantified over the wrong set and the hypotheses can never be satisfied, so the theorem is true for free. Lean is very happy to let you prove a meaningless thing with full confidence.

And then there's the Mathlib dimension. To specify a problem well you need to know how the library already represents these objects. If you define your own notion of "prime" or "continuous" instead of using the library's, you may have specified something subtly different, and you've also cut yourself off from all the existing theorems. So specification isn't just logic, it's a kind of fluency with a large and evolving codebase.

What I find interesting is that this is where a lot of the real mathematical thinking actually happens. People assume formalization is the boring clerical step after the math is done. In practice, writing the statement precisely is often where you discover that the informal problem was ambiguous, or that it had an edge case nobody considered. That's why I think specification, more than proof, is the bottleneck right now, both for humans and for AI systems working with Lean.

r001.rationale: The response says Lean requires precise types, domains, and explicit assumptions, and that translating an informal problem into a formal statement is difficult before proving it.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that writing down a mathematical statement already involves a lot of interpretation. On paper, we rely on shared conventions: what space we’re working in, what assumptions are implicit, or what we mean by two objects being the same. In Lean, you have to make those choices precise.

And you can write something that Lean accepts but that doesn’t actually express the problem you intended. Maybe you’ve added an assumption that makes the result trivial, or chosen a definition that leaves out an important case. So there are two separate questions: can you prove the formal statement, and is that formal statement a faithful translation of the mathematics? The second one requires a lot of care.

r001.rationale: The response describes making the choices and definitions behind a mathematical statement precise in Lean, and distinguishes that work from proving the formal statement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is that an informal mathematical statement leaves a lot implicit. We rely on context to know what objects we’re working with, what assumptions are in force, and even what a particular notation means. In Lean, those choices have to become explicit enough for the system to understand them.

And getting a statement to compile doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve formalized the problem you intended. You might accidentally make an assumption too strong, or choose a definition that changes the meaning. Lean can check that a proof establishes your formal statement, but the connection between that statement and the original mathematical question still requires careful human judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says that implicit mathematical choices, including definitions, must be made explicit in Lean to state the problem; it also distinguishes formulating and compiling that statement from proving it.
